summary.text: Cephalus the Aeolid hunter and Procris swore never to be untrue — but Dawn carried him off, jealousy returned in whispers of a rival named Aura, and the wife who followed her husband into the thicket died on his unerring javelin when he hurled at what he thought was game.

chapters.title: The vow
chapters.text: Cephalus son of Deion, king of Phocis, married Procris — Apollodorus and Pausanias call her daughter of Erechtheus, Hyginus daughter of Pandion — and they bound each other with oaths of fidelity. He loved the hunt above all; she loved him. Then Eos saw the hunter on the mountain and carried him away, and the marriage cracked under suspicion.

chapters.title: Aura
chapters.text: Ovid tells how reconciled lovers renewed their trust until a busybody heard Cephalus call upon the breeze — Aura, come — to cool him after the chase, and reported to Procris that a mistress shared the name. Hyginus instead has Aurora disguise the hunter to test his wife; either way Procris fled, won back gifts of the chase, and returned — yet doubt still gnawed.

chapters.title: The gifts
chapters.text: Apollodorus says Procris, after fleeing to Crete and sharing Minos' bed, received a dog that no beast could outrun and a dart that never missed — the same weapons Diana gives her in Hyginus when she sends the wife back to out-hunt her husband and win reconciliation. Cephalus prized both; Procris kept the javelin close.

chapters.title: The thicket
chapters.text: Procris followed her husband at dawn to spy on the rival Aura; when she rustled the leaves Cephalus, hearing movement, threw the unerring dart at what he took for a beast and pierced his wife. She died in his arms naming the innocent breeze; he learned too late that jealousy, not adultery, had brought them to the wood. Apollodorus adds the Areopagus and perpetual banishment; Ovid ends in grief and the tale told to Aeacus.
